papers.title: Imported Nationalism: How Foreign Influencers and Local Followers Amplify the Chinese Dream in Weibo’s Attention Economy
papers.category: 甲亢哥访华 · adjacent foreign-influencer mechanism
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: Using posts published by Western and non-Western influencers on Weibo during 2020–2021 and the comments of their Chinese followers, this study analyzes how foreign influencers articulate Chinese nationalist discourse and how local audiences amplify it through platform engagement. The analysis links comparative claims about China and the West to user-generated nationalism and to the incentives of the platform attention economy. It is adjacent rather than direct evidence for the IShowSpeed idea because it concerns domestic Chinese followers, not changes in foreign fans’ attitudes after a China visit.

papers.title: The dark side of GenAI in the workplace: technostress, loneliness, and the buffering role of transformational leadership
papers.authors: Fei Liu, Minxuan Qu, and Yixiao Zhang
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A survey of 290 public-school teachers in Taiwan tests a stressor-strain-outcome and conservation-of-resources model. GenAI-induced technostress is associated with lower work effort indirectly through greater work loneliness, while its direct association with effort is not significant. Transformational leadership weakens the negative link between loneliness and effort but does not significantly moderate the technostress-to-loneliness path or the overall moderated mediation. The cross-sectional design cannot establish causality, but the study directly connects workplace GenAI use with socio-emotional strain.

papers.title: Technostress and trust in AI mediate the association between AI adoption and employee well-being
papers.authors: K. D. V. Prasad, Ved Srinivas, Shivoham Singh, Hemant Kothari, Debanjan Nag, et al.
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A cross-sectional survey of 499 IT employees in AI-enabled organizations in Hyderabad, India, uses exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling. AI adoption is positively associated with psychological well-being and trust in AI while also increasing technostress. Technostress is negatively associated with well-being, trust is positively associated with well-being, and bootstrapped models indicate full mediation through both pathways. Because the study is observational and self-reported, the paths should not be read as causal effects.

toc.title: Seeing Is Believing? Most People Struggle to Detect AI-Generated Images
toc.abstractEn: A preregistered survey experiment finds that most people distinguish photorealistic AI-generated images from authentic images only around chance level, with modest advantages for younger, analytically minded, and experienced users.

toc.title: Webs of Ainu Mosir: Indigenous Creative Networks on YouTube
toc.abstractEn: A social-network analysis examines how Ainu creators use YouTube to form Indigenous creative networks and make cultural expression visible within platformed media systems.

toc.title: Social Media Platform Repertoires in Everyday Life: Measuring Social Media Use With Passive Metering
toc.abstractEn: Passive metering is used to measure how people combine multiple social platforms in everyday repertoires, addressing limitations of self-reports and single-platform behavioral data.

toc.title: Algorithms of Injustice: An Ethnographic Content Analysis of Black Youth’s Experiences with Racial Trauma Online
toc.abstractEn: An ethnographic content analysis documents how racially traumatic social-media content affects Black youths’ well-being and how platform systems participate in the circulation of that harm.

toc.title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
toc.abstractEn: The study adapts the discursive-opportunity framework to show how social bots alter visibility, resonance, and legitimacy in online protest discourse.

toc.title: Careful Dis/Connection: Bringing Digital (Inter)Dependent Relations Out From the Shadows of Autonomy
toc.abstractEn: A conceptual analysis argues that digital disconnection should be understood through interdependence and care rather than an ideal of autonomous withdrawal from devices and platforms.

toc.title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
toc.abstractEn: Three annual expert surveys assess agreement about the prevalence, spread, and effects of misinformation, identifying both areas of consensus and persistent uncertainty.

toc.title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
toc.abstractEn: Longitudinal and computational analyses examine which message cues predict perceived algorithm responsiveness and how those perceptions relate to later social-media use.

toc.title: Women Sustaining TikTok as Supplementary Information Infrastructure for Flexible Work Arrangements: Gendered Conditions, Community and Surveillance
toc.abstractEn: The study examines how women use TikTok as an informal information infrastructure for interpreting flexible work, while navigating gendered community support and surveillance.

toc.title: “I Share Your Sentiment”—A Longitudinal Study of Facebook Post Sentiment and Sharing
toc.abstractEn: A population-level analysis of Norwegian political parties’ Facebook posts from 2016 to 2025 tests how negative, positive, and neutral sentiment predicts sharing over time.

toc.title: Fandom Rupture in the Movement Society: Reactive Collective Participation Through Affective Practices
toc.abstractEn: The article explains how affective practices sustain movement-like participation after an external shock draws heterogeneous fandom actors into a shared platform arena before a collective goal has formed.

papers.title: Exploring enhanced self-esteem reactivity in response to social prediction errors in adolescence
papers.authors: Klara Gregorova, Geert-Jan Will, Pia Burkard, Marcel Romanos, et al.
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This open-access study examines how social experiences shape self-esteem in 141 participants aged 10–40 using an experimental social-evaluation task and ecological momentary assessment. In the experiment, self-esteem responses to unexpected social feedback follow a nonlinear age pattern and peak in late adolescence. In daily life, younger participants show stronger self-esteem reactivity to pleasant social interactions and naturalistic social prediction errors. Experimental and daily-life reactivity are associated, supporting heightened self-esteem malleability during adolescence.

papers.title: Interpretive incompleteness in global cultural flows: Ne Zha 2 and Labubu between visibility and decentralization
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A critical discourse analysis examines 349 media articles about the Chinese cultural icons Ne Zha 2 and Labubu. It identifies selective visibility followed by economic narratives that erase cultural subjecthood, political narratives that construct symbolic boundaries, and security narratives that recode popularity as social risk. The article argues that market visibility can coexist with limited interpretive power and proposes interpretive incompleteness as a structural feature of global cultural circulation. This is direct evidence about foreign media reception of Chinese cultural icons, but it analyzes media discourse rather than individual audience attitudes, identification, or sharing intentions.

papers.title: Selecting and testing cultural symbols for character IP: evidence from Mount Tai, China
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: The study combines expert scoring and an entropy-weight TOPSIS model with a structural equation model of 331 valid university-student questionnaires collected around Mount Tai. Anthropomorphic reinvention and emotional-compensation potential received the largest symbol-selection weights, while stronger cultural identity was associated with willingness to interact through new media and with cultural-tourism consumption. The self-report, hypothetical-stimulus design supports associations rather than causal claims. It is adjacent evidence because it studies domestic young audiences rather than foreign reception, but it directly separates resonance, identity, interaction, recommendation, and consumption outcomes for a Chinese character IP.
